opus-5.5.text:
I think synthetic data is very viable, but "mostly" is the key word, and you have to be honest about where the gap is.

My background is physical simulation, so I'm biased toward thinking simulation is useful. If you can simulate something, you can generate essentially unlimited data with perfect labels: exact geometry, materials, physics, every annotation you want for free. Real-world capture can't do that. For things like 3D, where good real data is scarce and expensive, synthetic data isn't optional. It's how you get scale at all.

The danger is the domain gap. Your model learns the distribution of your simulator, not the distribution of reality. If the renderer is a little too clean, or the physics is a little too idealized, the model will exploit those shortcuts and then fall apart on real inputs. So the question I always ask is: what is my simulator getting wrong, and does the model care about that error?

In practice, what works is a mix. You use synthetic data for scale and coverage, especially for long-tail cases that rarely show up in real data. Then you use a smaller amount of real data to anchor the model to reality, and you evaluate on real data, always. If your evaluation is also synthetic, you can fool yourself very easily.

There's also a newer version of this question: training models on data generated by other models. That works well for bootstrapping, but there's a risk of the system just feeding on its own outputs and slowly drifting or collapsing. You need some grounding signal from the real world, whether that's human feedback, real measurements, or a physics engine that actually enforces constraints.

So my view is that relying mostly on synthetic data is viable, and in many areas it's the only scalable path. But you can't rely only on it, and the quality of your simulator or generator becomes the ceiling. Investing in better simulation is investing in better data.

r001.rationale: The response says relying mostly on synthetic data is viable and often the only scalable path. It cautions against relying only on synthetic data, but does not assert that predominant reliance will not work.

fable-5.1.text:
Great question, and it's one I think about a lot because of where I come from. My background is in physically based simulation, you know, Taichi, differentiable rendering, that kind of thing. So I'm probably biased, but I think the answer depends entirely on what kind of synthetic data you mean and what you're trying to learn from it.

Let me split it into two buckets. The first is synthetic data generated by physics. Simulators, renderers, things where there's a real model of the world underneath. The second is synthetic data generated by another model, like an LLM producing training text for another LLM.

For the first bucket, I'm genuinely optimistic. If you want a robot to learn how a liquid sloshes, or how cloth drapes, or how light bounces off a wet surface, you can simulate millions of variations that would be impossible or absurdly expensive to collect in the real world. And the key thing is that physics gives you ground truth for free. You know the exact pose, the exact depth, the exact material. Real data never comes labeled that cleanly. So for perception and control in embodied settings, I think simulation will carry a lot of the weight, maybe most of it, with real data used mostly to close the sim-to-real gap.

But here's the honest caveat. Simulators are only as good as the physics and the asset diversity you put in. If your simulator can't model deformables, or your scene library has five hundred objects instead of five million, your model learns the simulator's blind spots. The gap doesn't disappear, it just moves to wherever your simulator is weakest. So "mostly synthetic" works when you're also investing heavily in making the simulator better, and when you keep a small but high-quality real dataset to tell you where the simulator is lying to you.

The second bucket, model-generated data, I'm more cautious about. There's good evidence that if you just loop a model's outputs back into itself without any external signal, the distribution narrows and you lose the tails. You get model collapse, or at least a kind of blandness. The cases where it works well are the ones where you have a verifier. Math with a checker, code with tests, anything where there's an objective reward. That's really just reinforcement learning with extra steps, and the "synthetic data" is valuable because of the verifier, not because of the generator.

So if I had to summarize: relying mostly on synthetic data is viable when the data comes from something that knows more than the model being trained, whether that's a physics engine or a verifier. It's not viable when the generator and the student share the same ignorance. And in both cases you still want some real data, not as the bulk of training, but as the thing that keeps you honest.

r001.rationale: The response says mostly synthetic data can be viable under certain conditions and limits its negative judgment to cases where the generator and student share the same ignorance; it does not assert that relying predominantly on synthetic data will not work.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on the task and how well you can reproduce the variation that matters in the real world. Synthetic data gives you a lot of control: you can generate labels, vary conditions, and create situations that would be difficult to collect. But generating more data doesn’t necessarily solve the problem if all of it shares the same blind spots.

So I would distinguish training mostly on synthetic data from validating only on synthetic data. The first can be viable; the second doesn’t tell you whether the system actually works in the real world. You still need real data to test your assumptions, identify the gaps, and guide what you generate next. The useful question is less about the percentage of synthetic data and more about whether it teaches the model the right things.

r001.rationale: The candidate says training mostly on synthetic data can be viable, provided it is validated with real data. It does not assert that predominant reliance will not work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on the task. If you have an environment where you can generate diverse examples and reliably check whether an answer is correct, synthetic data can be very powerful. You can produce a lot of training signal without labeling everything by hand.

The harder question is whether that data captures what you actually care about in the real world. A model can get very good at the world your generator creates and still struggle outside it. And generating more data doesn’t necessarily add more information if you’re repeating the same assumptions or mistakes.

So I’m optimistic about relying mostly on synthetic data in domains where we have good simulators or verifiable outcomes. But I would still keep real-world data and independent evaluations as an anchor. The important thing is the quality and coverage of the signal, not just how much data you can generate.

r001.rationale: The response says relying mostly on synthetic data can work in domains with good simulators or verifiable outcomes, while recommending real-world data as an anchor. It does not assert that predominant reliance will not work.
